title: At Long Last: Hawaiian Overthrow Episode
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom, requested by listener Kanaka Kai. They trace pre-contact Hawaii under chiefs and the kapu system, James Cook's arrival and death in 1779, Kamehameha I's unification with European weapons, the 1803 and later epidemics, the 1840s constitution, missionary influence, and migrant plantation labor. They then cover King Kalākaua and the 1887 Bayonet Constitution forced by the Hawaiian League, Queen Liliʻuokalani's attempt to restore monarchy power, the January 1893 coup by the Committee of Safety with US troops from the USS Boston, the provisional government under Sanford Dole, Cleveland's failed restoration effort, the Blount and Morgan reports, US annexation in 1898 under McKinley, statehood in 1959, and the 1993 apology bill and the Akaka Bill. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about blacksmithing and anvils.

segments.title: Opening and listener request
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners and dedicate the episode to Kanaka Kai, who asked for a Hawaiian overthrow episode. They preview that Hawaii's history raises questions about its statehood and current sentiment.

segments.title: Pre-contact Hawaii and kapu
segments.summary: Polynesian settlement of the islands and rule by chiefs who claimed divine origin. The kapu religious law system, its strict separation of men and women, and female rulers in Hawaiian history.

segments.title: James Cook arrives and dies
segments.summary: James Cook as the most notable early European visitor (with possible earlier Spanish and Japanese contact), the Sandwich Islands name, and Cook's aggressive behavior, kidnapping of a chief, and death in a battle on the beach.

segments.title: Kamehameha's rise and epidemics
segments.summary: Kamehameha rose after fighting the Europeans and used European weapons and support to unify the islands. Epidemics including an 1803 plague and a later measles outbreak killed large parts of the population, weakening defenses.

segments.title: Advisors, missionaries and the 1840s constitution
segments.summary: Kamehameha's Western advisors, and the arrival of Protestant missionaries who suppressed traditional religion. The first Hawaiian constitution, under Kamehameha III, replaced kapu with a Western-style framework including a legislature and judiciary.

segments.title: Plantations and migrant labor
segments.summary: European and American landowners pursued sandalwood, cattle and sugarcane, bringing in migrant Asian workers under exploitative conditions, described as a form of human trafficking.

segments.title: Succession disputes and Kalākaua
segments.summary: Succession problems and interregnums led to legislature-chosen rulers and riots. Kalākaua was voted in during 1874 amid a divided opposition supporting Queen Emma. He was known for reviving hula and for corruption, and he sought to restore royal power.

segments.title: Hawaiian League and Bayonet Constitution
segments.summary: The white-led Hawaiian League, backed by the armed Hawaiian Rifles, forced Kalākaua to sign the 1887 Bayonet Constitution, which made the monarch largely a figurehead and restricted voting to literate landowners, excluding most Asian laborers.

segments.title: Liliʻuokalani and the 1893 coup
segments.summary: Queen Liliʻuokalani sought to restore monarchy power and rewrite the constitution, prompting the Committee of Safety to act. After a policeman was shot, US Marines from the USS Boston landed. The queen yielded to the United States temporarily, and the provisional government under Sanford Dole was proclaimed with US minister John Stevens recognizing it.

segments.title: US inquiries and annexation
segments.summary: Cleveland sent James Blount, whose report found the coup illegal, and offered restoration only with amnesty, which the queen refused. Congress's John Tyler Morgan report disagreed. McKinley, favoring annexation, got Hawaii annexed as a territory, which ended the tariffs but not oversight of labor.

segments.title: Statehood, 1993 apology, and Akaka Bill
segments.summary: Hawaii's delayed statehood in 1959 due to elite resistance to losing immigration control and to growing Asian and Native Hawaiian voting power. The 1993 apology bill acknowledged Native Hawaiians never relinquished sovereignty. The Akaka Bill proposing tribal-style sovereignty was introduced in 2000 and has not passed.

segments.title: Listener mail on anvils and closing
segments.summary: Listener Nolan writes about blacksmithing and anvils, including the rebound test for a good anvil and the Peter Wright anvil. The hosts thank listeners and sign off.
